Mr. Speaker, as the House has disposed of the Orders of the Day, I will now proceed with the discussion of the question which I gave notice to the House I intended to bring up. I think it is most important that before we separate some cf the real facts in regard to the Alaskan boundary question should bo discussed in this House. I quite sympathize with the feelings of my colleagues who think that I might dispense with bringing the question up at this time ; but as there will be no other opportunity, I beg of them to stand the ordeal. In the newspapers of Canada, as well as in the private and public utterances of statesmen and important citizens, a good many things have been said on this question which might give birth to feelings between this country and the motherland as well as between this country and the United States which might just as well be avoided. In the first place, we must remember that the recent tribunal had nothing to do but to give a strictly legal interpretation of the treaty of 1825, concluded between Great Britain and Russia in regard to the line that should divide the Russian and British possessions in the North-west. The two questions which were raised before the tribunal were : What was the Portland channel through which the line had to pass before reaching the mainland ? and. what was the chain of mountains, or, in the absence of mountains, what was to be the line, dividing the British and the Russian possessions. and in what way would that affect access from the British possessions to the sea ? The Canadian claim was that if the line were drawn according to the real meaning of the treaty, we would be entitled to the ends of some of the deep inlets which penetrate through that strip of land, and which would give us access to the sea ; while the American contention was that the strip of territory which was acknowledged as being the Russian possession by the treaty of 1825, was to be uninterrupted, so that British subjects would be prevented from having access for the interior to the sea, except by river navigation through that strip of land. Of course, a good many contentions could be made, and have in fact been made, as to the interpretation of the treaty as it stands ; but the question put before this tribunal, as will be found in
the correspondence which has been laid on the Table of the House, so far as that strip of land is concerned, was, not simply what the letter of the treaty meant, but what was the intention of the parties who concluded the treaty of 1825 ? Well, Sir, if one only takes the trouble to go through the British blue-books and read carefully the corres-spondence that was exchanged for three years from 1822 to 1825, between Mr. George Canning, who was then Foreign Secretary in England, and Sir Charles Bagot, who was British ambassador at St. Petersburg, and afterwards with Mr. Stratford Canning, who succeeded Sir Charles Bagot, and who concluded the treaty, I' think no other conclusion can be drawn by any unbiased mind than that it was clearly the intention of the parties that the strip of land should be uninterrupted, and that Great Britain would not have any right whatever to the inlets that penetrated the coast.
Now, Sir, we must remember the facts of the ease as it stood at that time. The intention of Great Britain in opening these negotiations was not to delimit territory ; it was to obtain from the Russian government the repeal of Ukase of 1821, of Emperor Alexander, who had excluded all foreign vessels from navigating within 100 Italian miles of the shore of all territories claimed by Russia, whether in islands or on the mainland. Of course, that pretention was preposterous, and in the following year, at the congress of Verona, Lord Wellington endeavoured to have the Ukase repealed, but did not succeed. Joint action was taken by the United States and Great Britain to bring about the repeal of the Ukase, and for two years negotiations were carried on jointly between the Russian, British and American governments. But the Americans were as clever then as they are to-day, and they succeeded, while still apparently acting in conjunction with the British ambassador, in concluding a treaty with the Russian government without the knowledge of the British government ; and in the treaty concluded in 1824, the United States government acknowledged to Russia the right to bring her posessions down to 54 degrees 40 minutes north latitude. Naturally Great Britain was left in an awkward position, because the question of delimitation was thereby forced upon her, and the discussion began. To show that the British government did not care much about ter- . ritory or about that strip of land or its width, I will quote one sentence from the last despatch sent by George Canning to Sir Stratford Canning, in which he said :
It remains only, in recapitulation, to remind you of the origin and principles of this whole negotiation.
It is ' not ' on our part, essentially a negotiation about limits. It is a demand of the repeal of an offensive and unjustifiable arroga-tion of exclusive jurisdiction over an ocean of unmeasured extent; but a demand qualified and mitigated in its manner, in order that its jus-
Will the liou. gentleman read then the section which, according to him, provides that it shall follow the sinuosities of the coast ?

That is article 4, which I have just read. The words in the article seem clear enough, and, the letters and other documents make it clearer still. I do not wish to weary the House, hut I could give a dozen quotations, from George Canning, Bagot and others representing the British government, and from representatives of the Russian government as well, to- prove that, so far as the intentions of the parties are concerned, the object sought was to grant to Russia a strip ten marine leagues wide, not from the ocean, but from a line marking the sinuosities of the coast. The object of the portion of the treaty which I have read was only to prevent the Russian possessions from stretching too far inland.
Now, Sir, many facts have arisen since the signature of the treaty to prove what was the meaning the British authorities put upon the treaty, so far as that part of it is concerned. I can refer to official maps published by the British government which show that this reading of the treaty was recognized. I might refer to the case of a

prisoner who was captured by the Canadian authorities in Cassiar district. He was brought through, what was claimed American territory, but what we claimed to be our territory. He protested against being held as a prisoner while in American territory. He was tried at Victoria and was condemned. Not more than fourteen years after the signature of the treaty, (he one body of men most deeply interested in that country-in fact the only body that represented British interests in the country-tile Hudson's Bay Company (which company it must be remembered had political and military powers from the British government) made an agreement with the Russian American Company which also had political and military powers from the Russian government. These two companies signed an agreement in 1839, by which the Russian American Company leased to the Hudson's Bay Company most of that strip of coast for five years. The agreement was renewed for several periods of five years. And here is where the official part of it comes in.
When the Crimean war was declared, the two companies thought it advisable, in their mutual interest, to agree that a state of war should not exist in that part of the world. They renewed their lease and had it ratified officially by the British government and by the Russian government. After the war was over, as the members of this House know, there was a change of government in England, and the whole question of the Crimean war and its consequences were made the subject of inquiry. A committee of the House investigated' this agreement between the Hudson Bay Company and the Russian-American Company. Sir George Simpson, governor of the Hudson Bay Company, appeared before that committee and was asked what he knew of the nature and purpose of that agreement. He said that the nature and purpose of this agreement was that the Russians, having very little business now upon that coast, and the

Hudson Bay Company wishing to do some trade there the latter had leased the coast and got the lease ratified by the British government and by the Russian government, and agreed upon as being a neutral territory during the time of the war. He also produced a map before the House of Commons, and that map is still in the British archives, upon which he had painted in yellow the strip of coast granted by the Russian-American Company to the Hudson Bay Company. That strip of coast as painted upon that map is exactly the territory which is claimed by the American government and has been awarded to them by this tribunal. This is the map which was produced before the British House of Commons, accepted by the British government as showing the title of the Russian-American Company, and it was never contested by either the Canadian government or by the British government. I think this single fact should be sufficient to show that the line of demarcation between the strip of territory belonging to the Americans and the British territory, was acknowledged officially, and the territory outside of that line belonged to the Americans.

But aside from the intrinsic value of these islands, there is one feature of this incident which I think we cannot too much deplore as representatives of the people of Canada. It is the spirit which has characterized the decision of the majority of the commissioners, in so far as that part of the question is concerned. To my mind, instead of concentrating all our ire and indignation upon the shoulders of a worthy and learned magistrate, who, in regard to four-fifths of his opinions, had certainly facts to justify his decision, we should go to the root of things and find out where lies the real responsibility which has forced upon the people and government of Canada this unfortunate decision. That, I think, would be much more statesmanlike, and would lead to a much clearer and better understanding in the future as to our rights towards the British government. There were two means of disposing of this question-one by diplomacy and the other by judicial arbitration. If there had been an effort to effect a diplomatic compromise of this question, one would have had to have offered something in compensation ; and especially when dealing with a nation like the United States, I think it would have been a very dangerous thing to have gone to them and offered to compromise without having something to offer in compensation. We know too -much about their appetite and disposition. Perhaps hon. members of this House will remember that at the time of the denunciation of the Clayton-Bulwer treaty, I stated in this House that the moment the Clayton-Bulwer treaty was abrogated without compensation to Canada our case in regard to the Alaskan boundary was very much compromised. I was violently attacked at that time by some people who are now very hard on the British government and even on the British Crown. I could not explain at that time the whole of my mind, because I could not give public expression to my opinion of the Alaskan boundary question.

I had been connected with the Anglo-American commission to which the question had been submitted, and I could not speak ; but now that the Alaskan question is settled, I may say here what I had in my mind, and that is :	That the moment
Great Britain voluntarily decided not to set off the Alaskan boundary question against the abrogation of the Clayton-Bulwer treaty, our case was lost, because it was left for decision to judicial arbitration, and in my opinion, we had no ease from a judicial point of view. That was the opinion of the Hon. David Mills, late Minister of Justice, who published articles in England, stating that the British government had no right to denounce the Clayton-Bulwer treaty without obtaining for Canada a settlement of the Alaskan boundary question. So far as I am concerned, I declare here and now that I would have been the last man to ask Great Britain to give a quid pro quo as between the Clayton-Bulwer treaty and the Alaskan boundary treaty. I belong to that school of colonials who believe that we should ask nothing from the Motherland and give nothing to the Motherland, while at the same time we should preserve the very slight tie which has united us so far. But, Sir, I leave to my strong imperial friends ; I leave it to those who declare from time to time that we must make voluntary sacrifices for Great Britain ; I leave it to them to settle their account with the British government, and especially with Mr. Chamberlain, the Colonial Secretary, who, at that time, had in care the welfare of Canada. I may just point out en passant, that at a time when the sons of Canada were shedding their blood for the empire on the soil of Africa, Mr. Chamberlain was coldly sacrificing the interests of Canada, so far as they were involved in the Clayton-Bulwer treaty and the Alaskan boundary treaty. I repeat, that for my part I would not have asked the British Government to make the abrogation of one treaty dependent on the defining of the other. I think, Sir, that the British government should look to their own interests and that we should look to our own interests. But, as the same time, I point out this fact, to show those who think that the bond of empire should be an exchange of mutual services, that if they calmly study the history of the relations between Canada and the United States as affected by British diplomacy, they will find that the services have been very often on the one side, and the favours very seldom on the other.

To this Mr. Chamberlain replied that this was impossible, as the United States government would not consent. On the 18th of February, 1903, the anouncement came officially in a despatch from the Colonial Secretary to Lord Minto. The hon. gentleman means that Lord Minto acted on the advice of his ministers ?

Of course. To that despatch the British government replied that it was useless to make any representations at Washington, and they urged most strongly upon the Canadian government the acceptance of that tribunal. I say ' urged ' : the language of the British government is polite-they are always polite in their language-but the meaning is there ; and it is easy to see that the British government wanted to ' force ' on us the acceptance of that tribunal. But there was more to follow. A draft of the treaty was signed and ratified by the British government before they had obtained the final consent of the Canadian government to the constitution of the tribunal, as it had been announced by the government of the United States. Therefore, if we have indignation to express ; if we have sore feelings to give vent to ; let those who are so anxious about the dignity of Canada, not vent them upon Lord Alverstone, who, once appointed, had nothing left but to give a judgment acording to what he thought to be a strict law ; but let them go to the source of all the trouble ; let them go to the responsible statesmen in England who concluded a treaty affecting the interests of Canada without waiting for the opinion of the Canadian government representing the Canadian people. After the tribunal had been organized, there was no recourse but to have the question judged according to law. Lord Alverstone has himself pointed out that in his opinion the line of frontier, as provided for by the treaty, is an absurd one ; but he very properly added that he was not there to change treaties, but to interpret them. Then, Sir, so far as that is cpncerned, I must say that I believe Lord Alverstone has done his duty.
Now, on the broader question of British diplomacy, I want to be clearly understood. I do not say that the British government should take any risk in safe-guarding our interests at Washington. I do not belong to the school who would ask from Great Britain one iota of a sacrifice in order to protect Canadian interests ; but I think I have the right to ask, and every member of this House and every Canadian citizen has the right to ask, that the British government, for the sole purpose of catching American favour, shall have no right to compromise Canadian interests without the will of the Canadian people. That is all I ask from the British government.
Sir, if the members of this House want to have an idea of the great services rendered to the Canadian people at the hands of British diplomacy, in our relations with the United States, I will refer them to a little episode which happened in 1888. Wliat was the territory that was claimed, and by what title did we claim that the territory was ours ? The British Ambassador forgot to tell. The result was that the Secretary of State replied that he had never heard anything of the kind. The British Ambassador sent the reply to the foreign office, the foreign office sent it to the colonial office, the colonial office sent it to Sir Charles Tupper, and Sir Charles Tupper sent it to Sir John Macdonald; so that after four months of correspondence and red tape there was nothing left of our claim, and it was never known officially to the United States government that we had once in our life protested against their interpretation of the Treaty of 1825.
My conclusion from all this is that instead of throwing stones at magistrates, instead of complaining in an undignified way of the result of this award, we should take the position as it is, coldly and firmly, and learn from it this lesson, which is not the first nor the last, that if we want to deal with the American government, we should deal directly through an agent at Washington appointed by the Canadian government. Then, instead of it taking three months to have our letters sent to Washington, they could be sent in three days. I do not think I need add any more on this question; but being free, as I have been since this award was given, to speak my mind, which I was prevented from doing for the last five years, I thought I would give a piece of information to the House and the country in regard to what I consider to be the real facts of this case, so that we may draw clear and practical conclusions from the whole history of this Alaska boundary question.

Mr. Speaker, I do not wish to say very much on this question; but as this award affects my own constituency, and possibly takes away some of my voters, I can speak of it with a certain amount of feeling and possibly a certain degree of accuracy. The only reason why we should wish to have any frontier of Alaska, or any part of that country which is contiguous to our own, is because it is a gateway into the golden Yukon. We found in 1897, when gold was discovered in the Yukon, that we were in the position of a man attempting to do business in a store which had only a back door, the front door being closed. We could not get into our own store for the simple reason that somebody else commanded the entrance, and we were obliged to, go around by the back way. Prior to the finding of gold in the Yukon, there was little or nothing known of that Alaskan frontier. Skag-way and Dyea were not in existence, and they would not be in existence to-day had it not been for the discovery of gold in the Yukon country. The Lynn canal is useful only for ingress and egress for that country, though the navigation from Princess Royal 463i
Island up to the Lynn canal is decidedly dangerous on account of the icebergs which come out of Taku inlet and which are carried by the tide backwards and forwards. The terrible disaster which occurred two years ago south of Douglas island, causing the loss of the ill-fated ' Islander ' and the drowning of sixty or seventy people, is within the memory of every man in this House. Had our people been alive to the fact, as this House was, that we had a very knotty question to settle when the Teslin Lake and Telegraph Creek Railway was brought before this House, and had they forgotten the ordinary differences that exist between the two great parties in Canada, and joined together to carry through the railroad that was contemplated-I do not say anything of the question of route-there would be none of the soreness that exists to-day.
There would have been no necessity for an Alaskan boundary award and there would be no feeling in the hearts of the people of Canada to-day that any injustice had been done to them by that award. I do not wish to enter into a discussion of the merits of the case. I claim to be as loyal a Britisher as any man in the empire, but I also claim to be a Canadian and a business man, recognizing business principles as circumstances present themselves. We are face to face with a question, and we must meet it. We have a very rich country in the north, and are practically kept out of it today. The best thing we can do is not to question why we are placed in that position or the motives which led to the decision, but, recognizing the facts as they are, to take the best possible steps to improve' our present position. One hundred miles below Port Simpson we have one of the finest harbours on the Pacific coast, Kittn-maht harbour. During the present session I have had the pleasure of fathering a Bill granting a charter for what is called the Kittamaht harbour and Yukon railway. For the past four years many men in British Columbia whom I know, have recognized the difficulty presented to us as Canadians on account of being shut out from that country by the boundary award. We felt that such an award as has been given was bound to come, because we knew, as every man in this country knows, that whenever a question arose in which Canadian interests were at variance with American interests, Canadian interests were sacrificed to those of the American people, who, I might almost say are our hereditary enemies. I do not say that with any desire to be controversial, but we must recognize facts as they present themselves. We have seen this exemplified in the Ashburton treaty, the Oregon treaty, the San Juan Island affair, and now in the Alaskan boundary award-in every instance the interests of Canada were sacrificed. We know that there is no question about the San Juan treaty, and the Ashburton treaty, but the present

decision may have some controversial features, and I do not wish to go into it. We in British Columbia have always felt, perhaps more strongly than the people of the other provinces, that our interests have been sacrificed. In view of that fact, in view of our being shut out of the country, it behooves our government to undertake the construction of a railway from some point which we are perfectly assured cannot be contiguous to American territory. We must be able to discover such a point, for they cannot take anything more from us ; they have all that is coming to them. I do not think they should be permitted to take any more, and I would never be a party to giving any more Canadian territory to them. But as a loyal Britisher, 1 take the position that we must accept the situation as it is ; we are practical men and must go to work and overcome the practical difficulties that present themselves. To-day we see the Americans standing at the entrance of our Yukon country exacting tolls, trying to bring trade to their own country, and, recognizing that fact, we must seek a route of our own and be independent of them. Within one year of the construction of a road from Vancouver or Kittamaht harbour, it is immaterial which, the towns of Skagway and Dyea will slumber ; they will simply be a monument to the folly of the Americans in not doing the decent thing by us. There will be nothing in them, because there is nothing there to keep them except the trade going into the Yukon country. I would ask the government to consider the question very seriously ; to take it up from a Canadian standpoint, and to subsidize or to build a road from Kittamaht harbour or from Vancouver, north into the Yukon in order that we may be able to say to the Americans that they can keep their front door, that we have a front door of our own.

Now what took place after that ? An agitation arose in the United States, or rather an agitation existed in the United States with respect to the control by that country of the Nicaraguan canal. I have never expressed any such views and I have nothing to suggest on the line my hon. friend has just now mentioned. I am only contending that if the government of this country had suggested three Canadians instead of two-and three Canadians, impartial jurists of repute, could easily have been found- I tbink tbe imperial government would have accepted them, and I tbink we would have been absolutely justified in taking that course.
The next despatch, on the 7th of March, to Lord Minto from the Secretary of the Colonies, declares that the ratifications of the Alaskan Boundary Treaty were exchanged on the third instant, and it goes on to say :
Time for the preparation of the case, article No. 2, has consequently begun to run against us and it is important that composition of British half of court, also appointment of British agent should be settled without delay.
Hope,, therefore, your responsible advisers will favour us with their views on these appointments as early as possible.
To this despatch of the Colonial Secretary Lord Minto replied on the 2nd of March :
In view of the short time given for preparation of the case, my ministers desire to proceed immediately, and therefore suggest an early settlement of preliminaries.
As to the composition of tribunal, my ministers suggest Chief Justice of England and two Canadian judges, names to be .telegraphed hereafter.
As to counsel, my ministers desire that Mr. Edward Blake, K.C., London, and Mt. Christopher Robinson. K.C.. Toronto, be of counsel to uphold the British contention, and a junior counsel.
Under that clause of the treaty which provides for the appointment of an agent to represent each party before the tribunal, my ministers desire that Mr. Clifford Sifton, Canadian Minister of the Interior, be appointed to fill such position.
14S09

On the 17th of March Lord Minto telegraphed :
In addition to Chief Justice of England, my ministers propose Sir Louis JettS, a retired judge of the Superior Court of the province of Quebec and now Lieutenant Governor of Quebec, and Justice Armour of the Supreme Court of Canada, as members of the court of impartial jurists under treaty for settlement of boundary of Alaska.
That closes the correspondence as brought down. Now, Mr. Speaker, it seems to me that this government have not properly protected the interests of the country in the matter to which I have referred and which I will briefly summarize. In the first place, having declared their determination before the meeting of the Joint High Commission that this question would not be referred, on the part of Canada, to a tribunal the decision of which could not result in any settlement in favour of Canada and from which we could hope only a division of opinion, the government departed from that position without the consent of parliament or notice to parliament, and in doing so did not adequately protect the interests of Canada. I repeat that I cannot understand the reason which induced my right lion, friend, after he had given that pledge to the people of this country and to parliament, to consent to a treaty which was absolutely different from that arbitration which he insisted upon before the meeting of the Joint High Commission. What were the reasons that actuated my right hon. friend in taking that course, especially without notice to parliament, and in entering into a treaty dealing solely with Canadian interests without malting that treaty subject to ratification by the parliament of Canada. By what right did this government, after pledging itself to pai-liament that a certain attitude would be maintained, depart altogether from that attitude to which they were thus solemnly pledged, and which they had adopted in the first instance and consistently maintained with the assent of the British government before the Joint High Commission ? Lord Herscbell, representing the imjierial government. had resolutely taken this position, and he never wavered from it.
In the second, place, for what reason did this government take the attitude that this country had no direct interest in the Clay-ton-Bulwer treaty, and had no right to be heard in regard to the variation of that treaty ? Where is there a line of pretest on that subject addressed by this govern-ernment to the mother country 1 How comes it that without protest from this country the Clayton-Bulwer Treaty has been abrogated without any settlement of the Alaska boundary being coupled with it. How is it that my right hon. friend took the position that Canada was not interested in this treaty and that this government and the imperial government as well, departed from the position so distinctly laid down in the
despatch of Lord Landsdowne to the British Ambassador at Washington when the United States was pressing on the British government the necessity for some modification in that treaty ? I could understand the reasons which might induce the British government to seek to depart from the position It then took, but I cannot conceive any possible reason which would lead ' the government of my right hon. friend to depart from that position and to assume the position which the right hon. gentleman assumed in this House in the debate of last year. My right hon. friend then earnestly argued that there was no connection between the Clayton-Bulwer Treaty amendment and the settlement of the Alaska boundary question; that it was quite a proper course for the imperial	government	to	yield	to
the demands of the United States in the one case without insisting upon an equitable mode of settling the dispute which had arisen in the other case.
For the unfortunate result which this country has now to face, the government of my right hon. friend is responsible. My I right hon. friend is responsible himself, because if on the occasion I have mentioned the proper attitude had been firmly taken	we would	at	least	bein no worse	position to-day	than	wewere before; we would at least have had this matter open and we would not have been confronted with the absolute loss of practically everything for which Canada contended in this case. If the people of this country had been consulted in their parliament, if	this treaty	had	been	discussed by the representatives of the people in this parliament and if Canadians alone had been appointed on this tribunal, I believe that the feeling which has been engendered would have been very greatly minimized even in the case of the loss of outrights; and in questions of this kind, which touch the pride of the people, it is always desirable that if we are to lose, we shall lose in such a way that the people will feel that they have been consulted in the matter and that everything has been done to protect their rights which possibly could have been done by the government of this country. It does not seem to me that the situation will present itself to the people of this country in that way. I regret once more that, behind the back of parliament these proceedings were taken; that, without any consultation whatever with parliament my right hon. friend has seen fit to adopt a course, for which the government are absolutely responsible, and which has resulted so unfortunately for the best interests of Canada.

My hon. friend (Mr. Borden, Halifax) and myself, however much we may disagree as to certain phases of this question, agree ' in this-that the time has

not come to discuss tlie award which has been rendered in this matter. My hon. friend stated in his opening remarks that it was not advisable at this time-nor have we the information which would enable us -to comment upon the decision which has been given. But later on in his remarks my hon. friend stated that Canada would have probably have had more justice if three Canadians had been. appointed commissioners, rather than two Canadians and the Chief Justice of England. Perhaps my hon. friend is right; and, perhaps, in selecting the Chief Justice of England, as a jurist of repute, to pass upon these questions pending between the Canadian government and people and the British Crown on the one side, and the United States on the other side, we made a mistake-perhaps we should not have confided our interest to the highest expert in England. But, up to the present time, I fail to accept this view. I do not come to such an opinion as that yet, and I do not think we are in a position to maintain against the Chief Justice such harsh language as that which my hon. friend has just uttered.
speakername: The PRIME MINISTER (Rt. Hon. Sir Wilfrid Laurier).

speechtext: I hope the hon. gentleman (Rt. Hon. Sir Wilfrid Eaurier) will acquit me of using any harsh language towards the Chief Justice. 1 said that, subject to the consideration of the official reasons which might modify ray views, X could not at present imagine any reason for the course of the boundary around these islands. And if my right hon. friend can comprehend it, I shall be glad to hear his explanation.

But my hon. friend said also that we had made a mistake in not securing the appointment of three Canadians on this tribunal ; that we should have done better, that we should have had more justice, in that case, than we have had by the appointment of the Chief Justice of England. It is rather harsh to suggest that the Chief Justice of England has not treated us as justly as a Canadian would have done.
Does not the right hon. gentleman's language seem harsh with respect to the two Canadians who decided differently from the Chief Justice ?

I pass no opinion upon the decision of any, but I say there is an implication in the language of my hon. friend (Mr. Borden, Halifax), when he says that, in agreeing to the appointment of the Chief Justice of England, ye made a mistake-when he says fnat tfiree Canadians would have done justice where two Canadians and the Chief Justice of England have not done justice. I say that there is in that an implication against the Chief Justice of England. It is harsh language to use toward that gentleman, and I refuse to accept that criticism until we have before us the reasoned opinion of the Chief Justice, so Sir WILFRID LAURIER.
that we may know whether he is right or wrong. Much as I regret the decision, much as I am surprised at it, I will not pass criticism of that kind, nor suppose that the Chief Justice of England has given an opinion which would not have been given by a Canadian had that Canadian been in his" place.
I have said that I did not rise to express an opinion as to the value of the award. In my opinion, our case on the Lynn canal was not so weak as my hon. friend from Labelle (Mr. Bourassa) seems to think it, nor do I believe it to be as strong as has been represented by some hon. gentlemen on both sides of this House. So far as the Lynn canal is concerned, it seemed to me there was a case which was contentious, a case on which a good deal could be said on one side and a good deal on the other side. In reading the case, as it proceeded before the commission, I came to the conclusion that we had the best of the argument. Perhaps in that I was biassed ; perhaps I was taking a view which was not absolutely justified ; still, that was the opinion I formed. However, I never was free from doubt as to the strength of our case. I always admitted, in my own mind, that there was an argument to be made on the other side ; and, perhaps, our case was such a one as all lawyers have sometimes had experience of-when, going into court, they know that they may expect a decision on either side. But on the Portland canal, it seemed to me we had not only a strong case, but one beyond doubt, one in which there was no argument on the other side. Therefore, it is with surprise, with wonder, with astonishment, I find that the award, instead of giving us the whole of our contention, which seemed clear beyond all doubt, takes from us two islands which belong to us. These islands, I believe, do not in themselves amount to much-they are simply rocks. But they have great importance from the position in which they are. It is a great blow to Canadian interests, as I see them, that we are to lose those islands. But this is not the time to discuss that question. I would advise people to be calm and quiet until we have the whole case before us, so that we, every one, can apply his judgment to the merits of -the decision that has been rendered.
Nor is this the point dwelt upon by my hon. friend. The position lie takes to-day is that we made a mistake in agreeing to refer this question to the tribunal which has settled it. I differ from him, and I think I can make good the position the government took in this matter. The hon. gentleman referred to the position I took in this House more than once, that we would not depart from the position insisted upon before the Anglo-American Commission at Washington with regard to the terms of reference, if they were to involve any surrender of -territory. But what I want my hon. friend to agree to now is this-that he has failed to see the difference between this treaty and

the treaty concerning the Venezuela arbitration case. That which the British side wanted to have was a reference on the lines of the Venezuela treaty. This treaty involved a possible surrender of territory. It was agreed between Venezuela and Great Britain that if the territory of one was found in possession of the other, the territory could be given to the party in whose possession it was, under terms of compensation. For instance, it was agreed that possession for fifty years was to' constitute a title. Under such circumstances, there was to be compensation for the territory that had been taken possession of. We wished to have a similar provision in this treaty, and to provide that if the territory of one country was found to be in the possession of the other, the arbitrators would be at liberty to leave that territory in the hands that held it, subject to such compensation as might be found equitable. But this was not adopted. What would have been the consequence if it had been adopted ? Suppose that the town of Skagway had been found to be in British territory. That town is now in the possession of the Americans. It would have been in the power of the commissioners to allow this territory to remain in the hands of the Americans on such terms as seemed equitable to the commissioners.
That would follow a certain term of possession under the rules of the Venezuela treaty ?

Yes, the term of fifty years. But, at all events, it was to involve a surrender of territory. Under the award that has been given, Canada is to obtain two islands, Pearse and Wales, which have been in possession of the Americans against our protest. Under the Venezuela treaty it would have been in the power of the commissioners to allow these islands to remain in possession of the Americans under such conditions as they deemed equitable. But the present treaty provided a different rule altogether ; the present treaty provided on the one side and on the other that there should be no surrender of territory-and this is the mistake which has been made by my hon. friend. I would advise him to look again at the terms of the treaty, article I. of which enacts as follows :
A tribunal shall be immediately appointed to consider and decide the questions set forth in article 4 of this convention. The tribunal shall consist of six impartial jurists of repute who shall consider judicially the questions submitted to them, each of whom shall first subscribe an oath that he will impartially consider the arguments and evidence presented to the tribunal.
It was therefore a treaty which involved no surrender of territory. All that was referred to them was the duty of judicially interpreting the terms of the treaty. They were to sit as a court to determine, not what .one party was entitled to and what the other
party was entitled to-because under no circumstances could there be any surrender of territory by one side or the other-but to determine the meaning of the treaty. Under these circumstances, there was no necessity of referring such a treaty to parliament. If there had been any surrender of territory involved, it would have been not only important lout essential that the treaty should have been referred to parliament, because parliament alone can dispose of territory. Even under a treaty of arbitration which involves the surrender of territory, parliament alone can give its sanction to such treaty. But the only thing that was pro-videu for in this case was merely the creation of a court to determine judicially what was the boundary of Alaska by the treaty of 1885.
So far, therefore, our position is very different from what it was in 1899. What were we to do ? I have often regretted, Mr. Speaker, and never more than on the present occasion, that we are living beside a great neighbour who, I believe I can say without being deemed unfriendly to them, are very grasping in their national acts, and who are determined upon every occasion to get the best.in any agreement which they make. I have often regretted also that while they are a great and powerful nation, we are only a small colony, a growing colony, but still a colony. I have often regretted also that we have not in our own hands the treaty-making power, which would enable us to dispose of our own affairs. But in this matter we were dealing with a position that was forced upon us-we have not the treaty-making power. I am sorry to say that the whole correspondence which we have had upon this question since 1899 has not yet been placed before parliament; I am sorry not only that we have not the treaty-making power, but that we are not in such an independent position that it is in my power to place before parliament the whole of the correspondence as it passed between the Canadian government and the British government. But we shall have that correspondence, and it will be placed before parliament at the next session-the whole of it, no matter what protest may come from abroad, we shall have the whole of it. and then this country may know ex-actly*what has taken place, and what share of responsibility must rest upon each of the parties concerned in this matter. But we have no such power, our hands are tied to a large extent owing to the fact of our connection-which has its benefits, but which has also its disadvantages-the faet of our connection with the mother country making us not free agents, and obliging us to deal with questions affecting ourselves through the instrumentality of the British ambassador. *
The question came before us, and what were we to do ? Were we to leave that question forever an open one ? Were we to

leave that frontier forever a hone of contention ? Were we to leave a condition of things under which it might happen, in case of a discovery of gold being made in the disputed territory, that American miners and Canadian miners would rush in and a clash might occur which would eventuate in conflict and bloodshed, and difficulties which the mind shudders to contemplate ? We had to come to some conclusion, and after long negotiations which will be seen when the whole correspondence is brought down, we did decide upon this reference. The offer was made to us of accepting this treaty which implied a judicial interpretation of the treaty of 1825, the result of which could give nothing to our opponents and could take nothing away from us, but which would simply determine what were our rights under that treaty. I think it was the duty of the Canadian government to put an end to this unfortunate condition of things to which I have referred. That is the position which we took upon the case. We wanted to have the treaty judicially interpreted. We wanted no territory from the Americans, we wanted simply that which belonged to us. That was the proposition made to us, and we decided to accept it.
Now, after we had given our assent to this treaty, after we had consented to refer the question to this tribunal, which was to be composed of six impartial jurists, we were notified that the jurists which were to be appointed by the American government were gentlemen who, with all respect be it said, could not qualify as impartial jurists. JThey had expressed their opinions upon this question already with a good deal of emphasis. We protested against the appointment of these gentlemen, and we asked the British authorities to convey our protest to the president of the United States, representing that gentlemen who had expressed upon the floors of Congress opinions upon tliis question, could not come within the term ' impartial jurists,' such as were contemplated by the treaty. And, Sir. wliat took place ? Before our protest had been taken into consideration the treaty was ratified by the British authorities. Then another difficulty arose. What were we to do under those circumstances, the treaty having already been ratified ? His Majesty had given his [DOT] assent to it, His Majesty, who is the only person in the British empire who has a right to sanction a treaty. Under such circumstances what were we to do ? I want to know what our friends on the other side would have done. I ask my hon. friend the leader of the opposition what would have been their conduct on that occasion. What would have been the consequences if we had declined to give our assent ? The consequences probably would have beefl that the American authorities would have planted the American flag upon the disputed territory. and we would have been obliged either Sir WILFRID LAURIER.
to retire with disgrace, or to go to war to preserve our rights. That would have been the consequences. Therefore, we said : No, we will do the best we can in the condition of things in which we find ourselves. We confided our rights to the judgment of men who, we believed, were able to defend them before the tribunal. We thought that we could entrust our case to a commission of impartial jurists, who would judicially interpret that treaty. The proposition was made to us that the British government should appoint the Lord Chief Justice of England, Lord Alverstone, to represent the British side. Well, Sir, according to my bon. friend (Mr. Borden) I made a mistake. I confess that when it was proposed to us that we should have at the head of that commission the Lord Chief Justice of England, I thought that in the hands of a gentleman of his distinction our interests would be secure. My hon. friend suggests that I made a mistake, that we should have insisted upon the appointment of three Canadians instead of two ; he suggests that Canadian interests would have been more secure in the hands of three Canadians than in the hands of the Lord Chief Justice of England, associated with two Canadians. Now, Sir, this means, if it means anything, that the Lord Chief Justice of England, who was charged with the judicial intei'pretation of that treaty, did not judicially interpret it. but allowed Itself to be biassed by influences which it is a shame to mention or to suppose. If it means anything, it means that if the Lord Chief Justice of England could have judicially interpreted the terms of the treaty and apportioned the rights of the parties according to law and justice, then a Canadian would have gone against his conscience and reached a different conclusion.
Sir, I refuse to accept that proposition. But I believe, that, in submitting our rights to the Lord Chief Justice of England, we had every reason to suppose that our interests would be as safe as they could be in the hands of anybody, and that the government of Canada made no mistake in that respect. I would not be disposed to believe it at this moment. I shall wait until we have the reasoned opinion of the Lord Chief Justice of England. But, that is not the proposition ; that is not the remedy. It is not because we accepted one form of commission or another. I shall show a little later on where the remedy is. My hon. friend also made it a matter of reproach that we had accepted a tribunal of six instead of a tribunal of seven or of any odd number. It is true that we objected again and again to a tribunal composed of six members, but for what reason-not that there would not be as much justice in six as in seven, or nine, or five, or any other odd number, but because a tribunal consisting of six members, or of any even number, did not ensure to us that condition of finality which

we thought ought to be a condition of such a reference. If there were six commissioners there might be three on one side and three on the other side. If you had seven you would have an opportunity to have finality, but that is not an argument to show that we would have had any more security with seven than with six. Suppose there had been four commissioners opposed to us. Suppose there had been a seventh commissioner appointed by the republic of France, or by the Emperor of Germany, or by the King of Sweden, or by any other friendly power, and suppose that the seventh arbitrator had stood between Sir Louis Jettfi and Mr. Aylesworth, then the tribunal would have been composed of three commissioners on the one side and four on the other, and we would have been no more advanced than we are at this moment. Therefore there is nothing in that argument. The only thing that we feared in having a tribunal composed of six members was that there should uot be the condition of finality, but there is the condition of finality as the tribunal has been composed. But the difficulty is not there. The difficulty, as I conceive it to be, is that so long as Canada remains a dependency of the British Crown the present powers that we have are not sufficient for the maintenance of our rights. It is important that we should ask the British parliament for more extensive power, so that if ever we have to deal with matters of a similar nature again we shall deal with them in our own way, in our own fashion, according to the best light that we have.

May I ask my right hon. friend a question ? Did he not state, in regard to the colonial conference, during the debate on the address in the present session that the political relations were absolutely satisfactory and that no modifications of any kind were required 7

I stated that in so far as the relations between Canada and the empire with the view to an imperial federation or matters of a similar character were concerned, our relations were perfectly satisfactory, but I never stated that we should not have any more power in regard to our own autonomy. I stated that our relations were perfectly satisfactory, but I certainly never intimated that our powers should not be augmented in regard to treaty making. But, the hon. gentleman should remember that we have gained something if we have lost something by the treaty. It is important that we should be calm in regard to this matter. We have lost something, but we have not lost every thing. The Americans have not gained every thing they wanted. They have not gained everything they wanted on the Lynn canal, because, if they had, the boundary would not have been fixed at the summit of the White pass, but it would have been extended to 404
Lake Bennett. Moreover, on the Portland canal we have gained two islands. We have gained those parts of our contention if we have not gained everything. Such is the condition then that we have to deal with at this moment. It is not as bad as some parties are disposed to believe it is, but at all events it will be bad enough to cause us to look to the future to see what will be the condition and to try and remedy it. If there is a thing which I regret it is that in 1898 the Yukon Bill which was passed by this House was not permitted to become law. If the Yukon Bill had become law we would not have had this question confronting us at this moment. The White Pass Railway would in all probability not have been constructed and this Yukon Railway would have been extended to the Stikeen river, and from the Stikeen river to Observatory inlet, so that at this moment we would have had connection upon Canadian territory between Observatory inlet and the waters of the Yukon. But, that was not done. However, it is no use to look back to what is past It behooves us at an early day to see what steps should be taken to establish communication upon Canadian territory between the rest of the Dominion and the Yukon. I am not prepared to say what we should advocate. I am not prepared to say what we should recommend. But it is a question for all Canadians and they should be prepared for some sacrifice in order to establish communication between that distant part of our country and the more settled parts of Canada.

May I ask my right hon. friend if he did not say that he accepted as absolutely satisfactory the political relations existing between Canada and the mother country 7 Here is what he said:
As to the political relations which exist between Canada and the colonies generally and the mother land, they are perfectly satisfactory, they could not be improved, and any attempt which has been made with a view of improving them has cnly led to Utopia.

speakeroldname: Hon. J. I. TARTE (Montreal, St. Mary's).
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I was a member of the government when in 1899 the question of the Alaskan boundary was discussed before the joint high commission. A memorandum was then prepared. I hold it in my hand. It contains a statement of the different propositions that were debated then. The government of the United States declined positively to consent to an arbitration. The right hon. Prime Minister (Rt. Hon. Sir Wilfrid Laurier), who was, of course, the leading man on the Canadian side, in Washington, suggested an arbitration. Our United States friends suggested a commission of jurists. The right hon. Prime Minister, and the government, sided with him altogether, declined to accede to such a proposal. In point of fact I am within the memory of the House when I say that the

negotiations of tlie joint high commission were broken off on that point. The right lion, gentleman, at the opening of parliament, informed the country that the two governments being unable to agree on the Alaskan boundary the negotiations were broken off. That was the position when I ceased to be a member of the administration. We had exhausted every posible means of coming to some understanding. The government of Canada had offered to the government of the United States to give up what we thought were our rights to the Lynn canal provided we got the harbour on the Lynn canal which is called Pyramid harbour. The memorandum which I hold in my hand contains that statement. They declined to accept that offer.
Where is it published that our government consented to give up our right to the Lynn canal ?

During the negotiations that offer was made; it is a public offer. The government of Canada offered to renounce what they thought were our rights on the Lynn canal, provided they were given a harbour at Pyramid harbour. I believe I am responsible for that offer; 1 believe that under the circumstances it was a good offer.
We have no evidence of that published.
I am stating the facts. The United States government declined to accept our offer.
My hon. friend is all wrong there.
I am not wrong; I have the document here.
My hon. friend is referring to things which took place before the negotiations, and which resulted in nothing.
Are these pourparlers published.
I am not aware that they have ever been published.
I thought they had been.

It was a matter of common knowledge at the time, that the proposition was made, that Dyea should remain United States territory, but that Pyramid Harbour should be given to the Canadians as a free port, and that the United States commissioners considered it for a time, but it was rejected on account of strong opposition from the Pacific coast.
It was rumored that there was a compromise suggested between the two sides.
The newspapers reported at the time that the possession of

Pyramid Harbour was offered as a compromise, and that the United States refused to accept our proposal. They wanted a commission of jurists, and the Canadian government then broke off negotiations. In 1903, things took another turn. Negotiations for a reciprocity treaty were started- I do not say by this government officially- but by emissaries of this country-
If my hon. friend means that we started, any negotiations I dissent.
I have stated very distinctly that the government of this country did not start these negotiations but that emissaries from this country, important men from this country went to Washington
Name.

I shall. The hon. member for North Norfolk (Mr. Charlton) went to Washington and offered his good offices which were accepted, for a reunion of the Joint High Commission. The country has a right to know that at the very same time negotiations started again for the settlement of the Alaskan boundary question. Our American friends were so sure, that we were anxious for a treaty of reciprocity that they simply applied the screws. These are the facts of the case.
No, they are not.
These are the facts of the case.

I say no. I say that before Sir Michael Herbert's time, negotiations for the settlement of the Alaskan boundary were going on up to the time of Lord Paunceforte's death, and Sir Michael Herbert simply took up the continuation of them.

I say that the dates coincided exactly with the records of the case as we have them in our possession now. The negotiations started for a settlement in one way or another of the Alaskan boundary question. The right hon. gentleman has made a speech to-day which many of us are able to applaud. I cheerfully approve of some of his words. He has said that we have not been treated as we should have been. He is more than right in that. But he believed that when he consented to the appointment of the chief justice of England as one of these jurists, that our case was in safe hands. I fully appreciate his position. It is rather difficult for the Prime Minister of a British colony to say that our case was not safe in the hands of the chief justice of England; but we are confronted with the fact that the two agents appointed by the Prime Minister, men of high standing. Sir Louis Jette and Mr. Aylesworth ; they have stated over their own signatures-with the consent and knowledge of the government

of Canada I suppose-that the Chief Justice of England has not decided on judicial grounds. We are not making that statement here; it has been made in England over the signatures of the authorized agents of the Canadian government, and it has been circulated broadcast all over the world. Now, if the chief justice of England has not decided on judicial grounds, he has decided on some other grounds. The right lion, gentleman says that we have not ceded any territory. Permit me to ask him not to play on words. The contention of the Canadian government was that the boundary was to be thirty miles above the mouth of the Lynn canal, and they claimed the possession and ownership of the upper waters. But according to the decision of the tribunal, not only have we not the upper waters of the Lynn canal, but the frontier is thirty-five miles from the shore of these upper waters. If we are not losing and ceding territory by that, I do not know what we are doing. We are losing and ceding thirty-five miles, not of water, but of Canadian territory which we claimed to be ours. It has been said, and I believed it up to a few days ago, that this commission of jurists was not to decide finally. On that point the Prime Minister has not made himself clear. He stated at the opening of the session that the commission would not give any final judgment, but we are confronted to-day with the fact that the judgment is final. Our case is lost, the sentence is given, and it cannot be annulled. The right hon. gentleman also said that we have not enough power in these matters. Will he permit me to ask him what the consequences would have been, if when he found that the American government were in bad faith-because they were in bad faith-he and his colleagues had said :	We will not be a party
to that commission ?
My right hon. friend says we have not sufficient powers. If instead of appointing commissioners, under the circumstances that tun e been known to us, the government of Canada had taken a firm stand and had simply said to the government of England * He cannot possibly do anything, at any rate before meeting parliament. I believe they would have occupied safe ground. It was a new condition of affairs, which nobody suspected would exist. There was not a member of parliament, not a minister of the Crown, who a year ago would have believed we could have been treated as we have been. It was inconceivable that the British ambassador at Washington could have signed a treaty in which we were after all the only parties interested, without waiting for the answer of the Canadian government ; and, in my humble opinion, instead of saying to-day, when our case is lost, that our powers are not sufficient, the right hon. gentleman and his colleagues should have taken a firmer stand then, and should have told the English government: 404*
We cannot possibly take part in proceedings of that character. The Canadian people, and the British people themselves, would have applauded such a course. Of course, the Yukon, when it is looked at in the large map of the world in the Foreign Office or in the Colonial Office, in London, may not look very big. The English statesmen have to deal with large problems ; they deal with the affairs of the world ; and they are naturally anxious to remain at peace with all the friendly nations, perhaps especially with the United States. We all share in the desire to have peace with our neighbours ; but we have lost a great deal in our desire for peace-for commercial peace, for peace of all kinds. When the Clayton-Bulwer treaty was denounced, for the sake of peace we did not say a word ; we simply bowed our heads. A few weeks ago when Mr. Chamberlain started his campaign for preferential treatment with the colonies, some of the most important newspapers in the United States threatened us with the withdrawal of the bonding privilege if England would dare to give a preference to Canada. That is going a little too far. I beg to assure my right hon. friend that in the remarks I am making now, I am animated by no other desire than to make our position clear. I understand his position ; it is a difficult one. 1 do not feel inclined to blame him too much. I know that he was in a tight corner. The British government were asking him to give his assent. I know it is rather difficult for a governor of a British colony under such circumstances, to say : I will not do it. But would it not have been better, in the interests of the British empire itself, if such a stand had been taken ? Suppose that one of these mornings our American friends said, unless this or that is done, the bonding privilege shall be taken away from the Canadian people ? The more we yield, the more we shall be asked to yield. In my humble opinion the government should have taken a firmer stand. But it is not too late, after all, to improve our position. I quite share the views of the right hon. gentleman on this point, that if we had had the railway which was not built, perhaps we might have been in a better position. The Americans would not have felt that we were dependent upon them. We can now build railways to the Yukon ; but the position, commercially, will not of course be very good. If I remember well the distances,
I think it would be necessary to build about 800 miles of railway through the mountains. It is a long distance. We have spent large amount of money in improving the Lewes and Yukon rivers. We are completely shut out from all those waters. Now, I do not share at all the view expressed a day or two ago by an important newspaper published in Ottawa, that we must go on our knees to the Americans, and ask them to give us back those two small islands. Let us try to find another harbour. If the government
