act energetically, I believe they will get the support of men of all shades of politics. Let the government make up their minds to build the railway. Let them make up their minds once for all to be independent of the Americans, and the Canadian nation will cheer them. If I have been a little hot in my remarks, I say again that I have no desire to blame my former colleagues, but I believe they should have taken a firmer stand, and I want to impress- on them the desire of the Canadian people that the firm stand that ought to have been taken in the past should be taken now.
Let me conclude these few remarks by saying that what is true in this case is true commercially. The United States have been too much led to believe that we are dependent upon them commercially. They are selling to us millions and millions of dollars worth of merchandise, and they laugh at us. They simply take you by the throat every time they have a chance to do so. If we had grappled with them long ago, as we should have done, if we had raised the wall long ago, as we should have done, they would have been dealing with us in a different way. They would have been asking for concessions from us instead of taking us by the throat. Mr. Speaker, this incident which is a calamitous one, will have,
I hope, good results. The Canadian people feel badly over that award. They feel badly at the Chief Justice of England. It is a pity indeed ; but, after all, if the Chief Justice of England has not dealt judiciously with our case-and that is the statement of two men in whose honour and calmness I have great confidence, Sir Louis Jette and Mr. Ayleswortli-then, we have a right to feel sore at the Chief Justice of England, and it is our duty to say so. The right lion, gentleman has gone very far to-day, farther perhaps than any other Prime Minister has gone before. The Canadian people will not perhaps reproach him for that, because, being six millions of people, energetic people, we feel that we are quite capable of holding our own. We do not desire to attack anybody, but we feel confident that we can live and grow bigger. If we want to grow bigger, let us profit by this lession. Let us make ourselves independent of our American friends. Let us equip our harbours in winter and summer, so- as not to be afraid of the bonding privilege being taken away from us. Let us do it now. Let us arrange our tariff in such a way that they will understand that we can dispense with then-markets. We are not selling much to them. They are simply selling to us things which we can buy elsewhere. Let us make ourselves independent of them in every possible way, and let us see that our influence is felt in England. The affairs of Lug" land are conducted in the ordinary way of business. I am not sure that my hon. friends on the treasury benches have done everything that might have been done in that

respect. I say again it is not conceivable that the British ambassador at Washington would have dared to sign a treaty dealing with the interests of Canada without even waiting for the answer of the Canadian government. On that point the right hon. gentleman has not given the country the explanations that I believe we had a right to expect. He tells us that there is some correspondence which has not been yet published. Ministers of the Crown are, of course, not free to publish all the correspondence that passes under their eyes, but the country will feel more anxious than ever to see'the papers that have not as yet been published.

I have listened with much pleasure to the debate in many of its phases. I stand perhaps on a little different ground from a great many people in this House. I am an imperialist; I love the British empire and I hope that Canada and all the colonies will remain together for ever. I therefore think that I am in a little different position from the hon. member for Labelle (Mr. Bourassa) and I think he should not have interfered in this family quarrel. This is a family quarrel, and I will admit a Frenchman or a Dutchman or any other man who is loyal to this empire to interfere in this family quarrel. He himself is very civil and kindly but while I have been in this House he has imin-essed me with the idea-it may be untrue and if it is I will be glad to retract it-that he does not stand for the empire, but that his ambition is that Canada shall be torn away from this empire and form a little insignificant community by itself. I am expressing my sentiments and I will express them everywhere; if there were ten million people before me I would express my opinion. I speak with deference, but I do not think that in a matter of this kind the hon. member for Labelle (Mi. Bourassa) should intrude his opinions.
He is noti a member of the family.

He is but he has taken such a course with reference to the affairs of Canada that he ought not to intrude in this debate. I want to compliment the leader of the opposition on his speech. I think he has taken a strong, a patriotic and a national stand upon this question. I have often in this House attacked the imperial government. I did not attack the imperial government with a view to undermining that government, with a view of bringing about the separation of Canada and the other colonies from the empire, but because I believed in a household where brothers and sisters are growing up if they want a wholesome opinion they should at times sit down and criticise each other in order that the household may stand together before the world for weal or woe. Therefore when I

have attacked the policy of the British government it has not been to undermine British sentiment in this country, but to call the attention of the British public to the fact that they must change their policy in order to make it world-wide and sufficient to meet the new conditions that are growing up in this empire. The hon. member for Burrard (Mr. Macpherson) says that he should intrude in this debate because the territory in dispute touches his constituency. I want to tell him that this territory touches my constituency ; it touches the constituency of every man in Canada as much as the constituency of the gentleman who happens to locally represent it. It is Canadian territory, it is British territory and every man who owes allegiance to the flag is as much interested in that territory as the man who lives on its soil. I understand the doctrine of the hon. member for Labelle to be that Canada must not fight or serve the empire unless Canada is attacked. I say that Canada must serve the empire and stand for the empire if India or Australia is attacked, with the same energy and force as if Ottawa were attacked, and therefore I want the hon. member for Burrard to take a little broader view of this question than that it affects his constituency. I say that this affects deeply the interests of Canada and of the empire. It is the most vital question that has been settled in Canada for two centuries. We lost an enormous amount of territory in Maine and we know the difficulties which that loss has brought to Canada. Now on the Pacific coast we have lost 500 miles of the coast line of this country. Canada is only commencing her national career and already we are about to fling a line up to Tort Simpson on the southern extremity of this territory which we have lost. But when we want to fling a railway line two hundred or three hundred miles further north to develop this country we find that we are shut out from the sea-coast for 500 miles of our coast line. Canada is a commercial and a maritime country and no misfortune ever fell upon the country of a more grave character than that which lias fallen upon the people of Canada. Some people think it is bad enough to lose these islands, but what is that to losing 500 miles of the coast of your country which shuts you in ?
The hon. gentleman talks about a railway. A railway will help us out of our difficulty to some extent, but it can never help us in our trade upon the ocean. When the Pacific ocean is exploited, as it soon will be, and bears to Canada, perhaps more trade than the Atlantic, we shall be shut out from that ocean for 400 miles of the most important part of our coast because to-day trade is going north and therefore the United States commands the strategical point in regard to Canadian trade on the Pacific. I do not wish the disaster that has happened
to Canada to be minimized because it is a disaster which will grow in importance day by day ; but in every misfortune there is some silver lining to the cloud. I see some idle papers in the United States are talking about this disaster which has happened to Canada creating in this country a feeling in favour of the United States. Thank God it will create a bitter feeling towards the United States. Thank heaven that from this moment no man who is a Canadian will cherish anything but the most fearful dislike to the people who have wronged us out of our territory; thank heaven the idea of trade relations with the United States, thank heaven the idea of reciprocity will be killed in the minds of every Canadian. I say unhesitatingly, and I know; the question from top to bottom, that we have been wronged out of this territory, wronged absolutely wronged out of this territory. I believe that in my heart and therefore I see amid the difficulties that surround us, one good thing-that there will grow up in the hearts of the people of Canada a determination to have nothing to do with these people who have wronged us for one hundred years out of territory that justly belonged to this country and therefore I see in this award the destruction of all idea of a reciprocity treaty. I hope that now we will build up a tariff wall against these people and let them know we are Canadians.
I am afraid that is the mercantile argument.

I hope this disaster will bring us this compensation ; that is the only hope there is in the situation. Now, I want to deal with one or two of the difficulties raised by the Prime Minister. I think it is unfortunate that the Prime Minister has started the doctrine he has to-day in the interests of Canada. I would not mind the hon. member for Labelle starting this doctrine, but I think it is unfortunate that it should have been started by the Prime Minister of Canada. He endeavours to show that our difficulties have arisen because of our not having the treaty-making power. I want to tell the right hon. gentleman that this correspondence which I have under my hand shows that Canada has had the treatymaking power in relation to this matter just as fully as the imperial government. That is shown in every line of this correspondence, throughout all these negotiations. Let us look at the matter constitutionally. In theory, the treaty-making power is in the hands of the King, but the King exercises that power under the advice of his ministers, where the empire is concerned, where there is no self-governing parliament. But where there is a self-governing parliament, as in this country, the King exercises that power in conjunction with the ministers of the Crown in Canada, because the ministers of the Crown here ai<* as much ministers of the King of England

as tlie Prime Minister of England is a minister of the King. This parliament is charged with territorial jurisdiction over this country, and we are as much a part of the treaty-making power of this empire, so far as Canada is concerned, as is the imperial government. That, Sir, is the doctrine we must lay down in Canada. Therefore, I take issue with the Prime Minister, and I say it would be a vicious doctrine to advance, that the British government may make a treaty affecting the territory of Canada, against our will and consent. This treaty was made with the consent of the government of Canada, as much as it was with the consent of the government of England. Let us be fair and square in this matter. 1 am willing to place the blame upon the English government if they deserve it, and I have shown that wherever they deserve blame I have not been slow to blame them.
But when I blame the English government, let no man think I am blaming the English people. I admire the English people, because in this country we are all sprung, those of us who speak English, from the English, the Scotch or the Irish race. But, thank God, the most of us are sprung from them as they were 150 years ago, when they were a dominant race. But in the last 00 years that race has decayed. But that does not destroy the love and reverence we have for the British empire, by any means. What we have to do is to assist Joseph Chamberlain and the other public men, in dumping the present breed into the sea, and starting another generation of Englishmen, who will restore the splendid traditions of the British empire. I have never ceased drawing attention to the fact that the government of England does not, and has not for 60 years represented the great traditions of the British race. The English people are governed by a decadent class, which has grown up weak and impoverished in will. It is the. fault of Canada, it is the fault of Australia and, to some extent, of South Africa. We blame the imperial government, but you must recollect that up to within fifteen or twenty years Canada was regarded merely as a source of weakness to the British empire. There were stories told all over the world that we were drifting away from the empire, that we were drawing towards the United States. That being so, can we blame the British government for at times being weak in the presence of foreign powers ? Can we blame the empire, if, in the presence of her foes all over the world, when she was uncertain that her colonies would stand .by her in the hour of danger, she should faii to exhibit some of her old-time vigour and boldness ? Therefore, it does not lie in the mouth of the hon. member for Labelle, who is opposed to Canada standing up for the empire, to blame Mr. Chamberlain or any other man for not standing up for Canada. If Canada Mr. GOURLEV.
is not going to stand up for the empire, by what right can we require the empire to stand up for Canada ? I am prepared to require that the English government should stand up for Canada, because I am prepared to stand by the English government and empire in all corners of the earth. Therefore, I have always felt free to criticise the imperial government, and 1 feel free to criticise them to-day, and also to criticise this government for their action, and to hold them responsible for its consequences. Where there is a wrong committed in a British country there must be responsibility for it. Now, I want to make some comments upon the British government-not that we have any power over that government, but I want to point out to the people of England that their government has gone wrong in this matter, in order that the people of England may deal witli their government. I believe that when the people of England are aroused over this matter, as they are in Canada, they will deal with their government as we shall deal with our government, when the poeple sufficiently understand the pusillanimous course they, have pursued in this matter.
Now, let me proceed to say that the right hon. gentleman, in negotiating this treaty, was just as much responsible for it as Sir Michael Herbert or Mr. Joseph Chamberlain, or any other member of the British cabinet. The right hon. gentleman was a party to all of these negotiations from beginning to end, and at any moment he could have said : I will go no further with these negotiations-and there would have been an end of it. The British government says in this correspondence : If you don't agree, then all the negotiations must be broken off. They admitted the power of this government to determine these negotiations. Therefore, you not only had the treaty-making power, but you were the chief factor in the treaty-making power, so far as the boundary commission was concerned. Now, I think it is a little ungenerous for the Prime Minister to seek to arouse prejudice in this country by saying that we had not a right to change the complexion of this treaty. I say we had, and therefore it is that I point to this government as the occasion of the enormous humiliation to which the people of Canada have been subjected. I confess that I have been humiliated past endurance for a week, and I think every man in Canada must have felt the most bitter regret at the untoward and unfortunate events which have happened in this connection. But allow me to refer again to this correspondence and to another remark the Prime Minister made.

Mr. Speaker, when the House rose at six o'clock, I was endeavouring to show that the treaty-making power nominally rests with the King, that in England it was exercised under the advice of his ministers there, and, so far as Canada was concerned, it was exercised upon the joint advice of his ministers in England and his ministers In Canada. I had proceeded to show that in this case the British cabinet had abdicated their right to advise the King, and had constituted themselves a medium to hand the correspondence from Washington to the cabinet at Ottawa. This being the case, the responsibility for this treaty, in every respect, rests with the right lion, the Prime Minister and his government. And I think it was unfair of the right lion, the Prime Minister to suggest that the unfortunate result in this case was due to the fact that Canada had not the treaty-making power. The government of Canada has the treaty-making power in reference to Canada, and the territorial jurisdiction over Canada as fully as the government in England has the treaty-making power and territorial jurisdiction over the mere affairs of the United Kingdom. I want to show that the government of England made this treaty, step by step, on the advice of the cabinet at Ottawa. There is not a detail that appears in this treaty, that was suggested by the cabinet in Canada, that was not incorporated in the treaty. The government in England admitted the right of the cabinet at Ottawa to advise completely, in regard to this matter. This is proven by the correspondence. In the second letter, in the correspondence brought down, which is from Lord Minto, and addressed to Rt. Hon. Joseph Chamberlain, dated November 18tli, 1902, we find the following :
Referring to your despatch of 31st October concerning the proposal of the United States for the appointment of a tribunal of jurists to record their reasoned opinion on the Alaska boundary question, my ministers will decline to give final assent to such proposal.
Why, these words are In themselves an acknowledgment on the part of the ministers that they have the whole negotiations in their own hands :
My ministers would be disposed to consider it differently, provided reference to the tribunal should include all aspects of the question.
Then, we find, a few days afterwards, Sir Michael Herbert, in Washington, incorporated these identical words in his despatch to the Secretary of State in Washington. This despatch Is dated the 18th of December, just a month following the other :
My dear Mr. Secretary,-Since our interview this morning I have had time to examine the Alaska boundary treaty which you handed me. You will remember I told you that Lord Lans-downe was prepared to entertain favourably the idea of the tribunal, provided the terms of reference were so framed as to include all aspects of the question.
There is the identical language of the despatch by Lord Minto to the Colonial Office incorporated in the despatch to the British ambassador at Washington. This is only another proof that the British government admitted that, in reference to every aspect of this case, the ministry at Ottawa had the fullest rights. Therefore, I think it is very unfair, after the British government liad treated our government not merely with courtesy, but with a full acknowledgment of their'right to intervene in the negotiation of the treaty affecting the territory of Canada, for the right hon. Prime Minister to make the allusions he did. I do not wish to say anything unkind to any minister; but in a case so delicate as tliis one, a case in wliicb the words of the Prime Minister will have very special weight in forming and guiding public opinion, I cannot but think his utterance was unfair to His Majesty's ministers in England.
I was astonished to hear the right hon. Prime Minister make the declaration that Canada had not the treaty-making power. While, of course, that power is nominally in the King, yet the King exercises it upon the advice of his ministers. The ministers in England might, I will admit, arbitrarily refuse to allow the advice of ministers of the Crown in Canada to have weight. But, if they did that for an instant, the whole organization of the empire would be upset, and this people would question that right before we took another step in connection with the empire. I bad known always that the government of Canada was consulted fully in every matter with reference to treaty-making since confederation. Sir John Macdonald, when Prime Minister was not only consulted, but was made one of the high commissioners to negotiate the treaty of Washington. And that treaty was made subject to the ratification of this parliament -the most complete acknowledgment, on behalf of the Crown, that the treaty-making power, so far as it refers to the territory of Canada, rested as completely with the parliament of Canada as the treaty-making power in relation to the United Kingdom, rested with the imperial parliament. I appeal to any constitutional lawyer in Canada to say if that is not the correct interpretation of the constitution of the empire at the present time. Had any other interpretation been attempted, had the right of the Canadian ministry to advise on this subject been questioned tlie right hon. Prime Minister could have followed the lead of Cecil Rhodes. Twenty-five years ago the German empire laid hands upon a part of the British empire in British South Africa, trusting to the weakness of the British cabinet, and tlie hesitation of the ministry to meet these aggressions with an ultimatum, under which Germany would have backed down so quickly that there would have been no time to raise a question. But the British government weakly permitted Germany to appro-

m
priate a part of South-west Africa. Then, Germany advanced her posts and took Bech-uanaland, the design being to cross and join hands with the Boers, which would have cut off the extension of British influence to the north, and would have confined British South Africa to a little strip around the cape. The ministers in England acted supinely. They set no particular value upon South Africa. The cabinet in South Africa spent days and days in cabling, endeavouring to get the British government to take direct and positive action to drive Germany out of Bechuanaland. Receiving no satisfaction, they acted. Under the inspiration and leadership of Cecil Rhodes, that government passed a minute of council and transmitted it to the ministers in England, telling them that if the British Crown would not defend South Africa to pull down their flag. Cape Colony would float its own flag, and would fight Germany alone and singlehanded. In an hour came back the answer that fleets would sail and armies would move to save South Africa. Cecil Rhodes solved that question then and there, that, so far as a British colony is concerned, the government of the colony was supreme in power in dictating its policy.
That was twenty-five years ago and if it had not been for that splendid attitude of Cecil Rhodes, the Boers would have united with the Germans in South Africa and the whole domain that we own in South Africa would have been appropriated by the German Empire. Cecil Rhodes had to act the part of a hero and had to act the part of a man with a dominant mind in his dealings with the imperial government. In this instance how differently was the right lion. Prime Minister treated. The right bon. Prime Minister might have followed that distinguished precedent in the negotiations leading up to the composition of the tribunal. but it was not necessary, because, in these negotiations, the government of England only acted as an intermediary to hand the correspondence from Washington to the government at Ottawa. The government at Ottawa alone are responsible for the negotiations leading up to this treaty. As we come to understand the matter better the people know that, and no amount of misrepresentation will avail to colour the situation one jot or tittle. The people of Canada are intelligent and they will soon come to know the truth. They will read the correspondence and they will know exactly the position we are in. I must say that I was amazed when I heard the right hon. Prime Minister undertake to defend himself. Instead of guiding the hon. member for Labelle, instead of telling that young man that he was pursuing a wrong course in this country, a course that could not commend itself to the English or the French speaking people, he encouraged him in it. I believe that the feeling is growing so strong in Canada that there will not be

the slightest distinction between French and English in their devotion to the empire. Occasionally they get a bad leader in the province of Quebec and a bad leader can perhaps work more evil there than a bad leader can in one of the English speaking provinces, but I believe the people of Quebec are sound at heart and that though they are misled by the hon. member for Labelle they will go in the right way. Instead of making himself strong in this empire that hon. gentleman will make himself a false guide of public sentiment everywhere and therefore the right hon. Prime Minister, to whom we must look to direct public sentiment in correct channels, should have repudiated the statement of that hon. gentleman that we had not the treaty-making right and that we had been sacrificed by Chamberlain. Chamberlain has done more for this empire in half an hour than a million of hon. members for Labelle could do in a million years. I am afraid that the hon. gentleman is not sincerely interested in the welfare of Canada. I may be wrong, but we have a right to judge men's hearts by the conduct they exhibit and that is my conclusion in reference to the hon. member for Labelle. I hope I am wrong. I do not wish to say that there is any man in Canada who entertains any opinion that it is improper for him to entertain as a citizen of this country, but I am bound to come to a common sense conclusion in reference to a man's heart from the conduct which he manifests. That is my conclusion in reference to the hon. member for Labelle, and it must be the conclusion of the right lion, the Prime Minister, who has had more intimate associations with the hon. gentleman than I have had. Instead of encouraging him in that line of argument he should have depreciated it. He should have said : The government of England gave us the freest hand in reference to this treaty' and if there is a mistake the government of Canada is prepared to shoulder it and to meet the people of this country on that issue. I am sorry to have to charge either the government of England or this government with dereliction in this respect but I am much more pleased to be able to charge this government than the imperial government with it, because, if we were to charge the imperial government with this matter, it would create a profoundly injurious feeling in the empire. But, this government, I find from reading this correspondence, are alone responsible for the whole difficulty that has occurred. The right hon. Prime Minister has sought to shield himself behind the name of Lord Chief Justice Alverstone as if that would help the situation. There have been many chief justices of England who have illustrated the genius of the English race and there have been many other chief justices of England who have illustrated the worst features of English character and life. There have been some very learned chief justices

and there have been some-I speak as a lawyer familiar with the law courts of England-who are no more worthy of respect than any judge in Canada, in reference to the Lord Chief Justice of England I would rather have had the Chief Justice of Nova Scotia on that tribunal, or I would rather have had the Chief Justice of British Columbia than the Lord Chief Justice of England. I will frankly say that as a Canadian I believe that there is more will power and active business capacity about a Canadian than about any Englishman be he Lord Chief Justice or Prime Minister. I believe that the average intelligence of the Canadian is infinitely ahead of the average intelligence of the Englishmen in the same rank of life, and I believe that the ordinary lawyer in Canada is all round a much better man than the average lawyer in England. I say that with all respect to the British empire and as a devoted imperialist. We have the highest civilization that exists in the whole world and I believe that more general intelligence exists in Canada than exists in any other country in the world. I have said that the right lion. Prime Minister attempted to shield himself behind the name of the Lord Chief Justice of England. I am not concerned in defending the Lord Chief Justice of England nor am I concerned in attacking him. I think the proper course to take is the course which the hon. leader of the opposition (Mr. Borden, Halifax) took, to await the opinion which is said to have been delivered by the Lord Chief Justice. We have no right to condemn any man upon a general opinion until we know the reasons upon which it is founded. When I get the reasons upon which he founded that opinion I will criticise it with the same freedom as if it were the opinion of any mechanic or cabman in the city of Ottawa. X will not be deterred from criticising his opinion any more than I would be from criticising the opinion of any lawyer or judge in Canada. If the right hon. gentleman had consulted men like the Chief Justice of Nova Scotia, a highlander who would have faced these boasting Yankees and told them that they had enough of the territory of Canada and that they couldi not get another foot of it, the result might have been different. He would not have yielded and he would have brought as much intelligence and discrimination to bear upon the case as the Lord Chief Justice of England. As a Canadian I think that the hon. member for Labelle did not do justice to the position that our Canadian jurists occupy in this country. X am willing that Englishmen shall have all the credit they deserve but I want to put forth the claim that we have lawyers in Canada who occupy a position as high as that of any lawyer in the world. There is no divine superiority for any man because he happens to reside in England. This case is res judicata. On the side of Canada there were three arbitrators. Two of them decided in favour of Canada and therefore Lord Alverstone is the dissenting arbitrator. The majority of the court on Canada's side decided against Lord Alverstone and he should have accepted that decision on the part of Canada. The tribunal as far as Canada is concerned was composed of three members and the majority of the tribunal representing Canada decided in favour of Canada from the facts which they had heard. I shall not imitate the hon. member for Labelle and undertake to review the case. I do not know whether he is a lawyer or not, but I think he followed a very foolish course. This whole matter was left to the court, all the facts have been presented to it, and the members of the tribunal have rendered their judgment. I am bound to believe that Lord Alverstone was wrong and I am bound to accept the decision of the majority of the court composed of Canadians as being the proper one.
I am bound by the majority opinion of the court, and consequently, X must conclude that Lord Alverstone is wrong. I do not know either Sir Louis Jette or Mr. Ayles-worth, and I am not concerned to compliment or eulogize them, but they were chosen by the government of Canada for a very high judicial mission ; they heard the full argument as well as Lord Alverstone, they decided in favour of Canada, and I believe that their decision is right. If two English judges had decided a question against a Canadian judge, fancy Englishmen having the slightest doubt as to who was right. So far as Lord Alverstone's opinion is concerned, the thing is res judicata; Canada was right and Lord Alverstone improperly decided against her interests. We must inferentially conclude that Lord Alverstone was wrong, but we have in addition the statement of Mr. Aylesworth, who knows all the facts, that the judgment was not come to upon judicial grounds. lord Alverstone occupies the unenviable position therefore of being condemned twice over. Judges must submit to criticism, and Lord Alverstone, the lord Chief Justice of England, must not escape criticism any more than if he were the lord Chief Justice of Timbuctoo. I am bound as a Canadian, to accept the decision of the two eminent Canadians who were thought worthy to sit in this tribunal, and accepting their decision, I am bound to hold that Canada was not properly supported by Lord Alverstone. Mr. Ayleswortk's dissenting opinion occupies three columns of the ' Times,' and in that opinion he says :
I have merely to say that the course the majority of the tribunal has decided to take with regard to the islands at the entrance of the Portland canal is in my humble opinion so opposed to the plain requirements of justice.
If one of the judges was free to discuss Ijord Alverstone, thus, surely, I am relieved

from any qualms when 1 discuss his conduct here.
-is in my humble opinion so opposed to the plain requirements of justice and so absolutely irreconciliable with any disposition of any branch of the case, upon principles of a judicial character, that I respectfully decline to affix my signature to it. [DOT]
For a lawyer, trained to use language in a constrained sense, that is a most powerful indictment of Ford Alverstone. I have never been in England, although some of my family live there. However, from knee-high, English papers flooded my home, and before I knew anything about Canadian papers, I became, more or less saturated with English public opinion. I have read the diplomatic correspondence of this empire for seventy or eighty years, and I know that for sixty years the diplomacy of England has been chiefly marked by a desire to avoid war at any cost. Why, in the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries Englishmen would have shot off their guns and sent out their ships, and retribution would follow any who dared to touch part of the empire. Let me say incidentally, that the iniquitous free trade doctrine that Cobden introduced lias degraded the public sentiment ol' England. It seems to strike the very heart of Englishmen and to degrade them. In the history of Great Britain there is a mark, as pronounced as if a mountain range had been erected, to divide the period between sixty years ago and afterwards. There has been evidence of a marked decadence of the great spirit, that once told the world : Don't touch our territory, or we will seek redress with our ships, our arms, and our men. With the era of free trade the most marked indications of decay set in. Germany could steal British territory, the United States could flout her in the face, France could do likewise, and England would bow. That Js not the fault of the British empire, hut it is tlie fault of the weak and impoverished race that is living in England at the present day. England has got vastly rich in the last sixty years, the merchants of England find tlieir ships bearing them wealth from every corner of the earth, and the English government lias got under the control of the rich merchants and the Jews of London, and whenever her territory is assailed, instead of being revenged these men of commerce say : Take the kicks and the jibes and the outrages of fortune, but don't declare war, because if you do, we may lose 8100. And so, England that in the past was honoured the world over, lost her honour, because every nation in the world knew that she would not fight. Let it go abroad that a nation will not fig'ht for her territory and her rights, and every nation in the world will attack her. But, let it be known that the smallest nation on earth will defend her territory, and she is honoured and respected. Look at the history of Switzerland, a little country with a million people, Mr. GOURLEY.
which for three hundred years has defied every power in Europe. She is honoured and respected by the great nations, because every nation knows that if Switzerland is attacked it will be a war of extermination. Switzerland maintains her independence today because of her pluck, and a daring and courage, while England with all her wealth, has been buffeted by every nation of the world. The Prime Minister knew the diplomacy of England, and especially her diplomacy in reference to the United States.
I am a strong imperialist, but I have been trying to bring public opinion to bear upon the unworthy people of England to-day, to let them know that the time is past for subserviency, and that while the people of the old country may submit to humiliation, we in this young country never shall. No matter how degenerate men may be in England, when the race breathe the free air of Canada, they become regenerated. It is impossible for us to bow to humiliation. I want to find out who is responsible for the appointment of Lord Alverstone, and I am happy to say that this correspondence points out to me clearly that the whole error lies at the door of the government of Canada, so that I am pleased to find that the member for Labelle (Mr. Bourassa) was wrong in trying to mislead the people of Canada to think otherwise.
With reference to the treaty, I find that when it was sent out to Canada a very important alteration was made in it. That would have given the right hon. the Prime Minister ample opportunity to have said at once : This treaty does not preserve the rights of Canada which were given to us by the treaty made between England and Russia in 1S25. In that treaty there was a clear boundary established. If the arbitrators had not been allowed to alter that boundary, there would have been no doubt as to the decision ; and I venture to say that when the opinion of Lord Alverstone comes to this country, it will be found that it is based upon the change that was made in the treaty with the consent of the Prime Minister of Canada. In the old treaty made between Russia and England in 1825 the boundary was set out as clearly as words could define it. The boundary was never at any time to exceed ten marine league's, or thirty miles, from the coast. Mountains were referred to, but only in case they should be within ten marine leagues of the coast. But what happened ? The United States knew that if that question were submitted to a tribunal the decision would be against them, and what did they do ? When the treaty of arbitration was made, they had a clause put into it which enabled that tribunal to take into consideration matters which had happened before and after the treaty was committed to writing. Everybody knows that when nations get together to make a contract a number of discussion^ occur. One nation claims this or that ; but in the end, when

the matter is committed to writing and the treaty is once ratified, you cannot go outside of the terms of that treaty. Everything is in it, and it is simply a matter of the interpretation of the words, unless there is found to^ be some latent ambiguity requiring explanations. In this case it is not pretended that there was any ambiguity. The language was clear and distinct, and if that treaty had been submitted to a judge, even to Lord Alverstone, and he had been bound down by the simple words of the treaty, we would never have lost the two islands, but would have preserved our rights intact. But when the treaty of arbitration was sent out this extraordinary clause was found in, which was no doubt cited by Lord Alverstone in coming to his decision. A draft of the treaty was sent to this government, and I have no doubt that this government must have acted in concert with the English government in order to help them out of this difficulty. The clause I refer to is as follows :
The tribunal shall also take into consideration any action ot the several governments or their respective representatives preliminary or subsequent to the conclusion of said treaties, so far as the same tends to show the original and effective understanding of the parties in respect to the limits of their several territorial jurisdictions under and by virtue of the provisions of said treaties.
Under that clause of the treaty Lord Alverstone could throw away the treaty on which we had relied for our rights with regard to the boundary, and could listen to all the cock-and-bull stories set up by the Americans with reference to what had taken place before and after the treaty, and could found his decision upon them. The government of Canada could have insisted that our rights should be preserved in the fullest manner by the treaty, which fixed the boundary in such a way -that no court could get over them. I went over this whole matter for a couple of months with the late Mr. Justice Mills. We happened to lodge together in the Russell House, and we went over this matter night after night, and I had-the benefit of his vast information on the whole subject. I found him better informed on this question than any Canadian I have since met, and it was his opinion that under the terms of the old treaty the United States had not a leg to stand upon. I hold that the first mistake of the government of Canada was in permitting the introduction of a clause like that, which struck at the very foundation of the article in the treaty by which our rights were secured.
Then, in the appointment of the commissioners the Prime Minister was not taken by surprise. I find by this correspondence that as soon as the American commissioners were appointed he was informed of their appointment. He knew that the English government had departed entirely from their notion of having six jurists to deal with the
matter ; and when the names of the United States jurists were submitted, the most ample opportunity was afforded -to the government of Canada of stepping out and refusing to go any further. I am boun'd to say that the government of Canada did remonstrate against the American commissioners. But what happened ? Here is the most ample evidence that the government of. England said at once : If you object to these people the negotiations will be abandoned. What more could the government of Canada want ? I understood the Prime Minister to allege to-day that the treaty had then been signed. No matter whether it had been signed or not. Here are the words of the British government :
His Majesty's government have therefore to choose between breaking off negotiations altogether or accepting American nominations and appointing as colleagues representatives who will meet -the altered circumstances of the case.
His Majesty's government say that they have nothing to do but to break off the negotiations if the Canadian government object to the American commissioners. That was all that was necessary ; they would have had to say to the American government that if. they did not keep their agreement with reference to the appointment of jurists the treaty was off, because that was the very basis of the negotiations. But there seems to have been some secret influence working from London on the government of Canada, because what they rejected by one mail they accepted by the next. We find that the Prime Minister withdrew his objection and suggested the name of Lord Alverstone as one of the British commissioners. I saw that by a paper in London it is made to appear that Lord Aiverston-e's appointment was forced on the government of Canada by the English government, and I inferred' that from what the hon. member for Labelle said. I see that the matter is being discussed in England :
The 'Morning Post ' recalls the earnest recommendation of Sir Richard Webb in March last that the British commissioners be all Canadians, arguing the appointment of a single Englishman to be unjust to Canada and impolitic for the empire. The ' Post ' asks, presumably with some ulterior purpose : ' Has the British government evidence that Canada was anxious above all for a verdict, and also that the Canadian government approved of the selection of an Englishman as a commissioner ?'
The English ' Post ' suggests that some people here were so anxious for a verdit that they were willing to sacrifice the interests of Canada for the purpose of getting a verdict, and willing to take anybody as a commissioner. It asks if there is evidence that the Canadian government nominated Lord Alverstone. I am bound to say that the evidence is here. Lord Alverstone is the nominee of Canada, he was our appointment. If he was our appointment, we should acknowledge that fact and should not leave any doubt about the matter in the English

public mind. I find in a despatch of Lord Minto to the Colonial Office the following
passage
In view of the short time given for the preparation of the case, my ministers desire to proceed immediately, and therefore suggest an early settlement of preliminaries.^ As to the composition of the tribunal my ministers suggest the Chief Justice of England and two Canadian judges, names to be telegraphed hereafter.
Then the despatch proceeds to name the counsel who are to carry on the arbitration for Canada. I want to know from the Prime Minister why three Canadians were not nominated. I observe that Sir Richard Webb, in the Colonial Office urged upon this government or the Imperial government, that there should be three Canadian commissioners. Who is Sir Richard Webb ?
I do not know, and there is no foundation at all for this statement.
Is he connected with the Colonial Office ?

I do not know him at all.
' Mr. GOURLEY. Did you know of him in connection with the correspondence ?
I did not.

I see in this despatch :
The * Post' recalls the earnest recommendation of Sir Richard Webb, in March last, that the British commissioners be all Canadians, arguing the appointment of a single Englishman to be unjust to Canada and to the interests of the empire.
If Sir Richard Webb made such a recommendation to the British authorities it Was never conveyed to us.

I cannot imagine why, in a case of this kind, three Canadians were not selected ; it is a reflection on the people of Canada that the three commissioners should not have been chosen from Canada. Had it been 500 miles of the coast of England along the channel or the North Sea, which had been claimed by France, do you suppose that England would agree to the appointment of two Englishmen and one Canadian as a board of arbitration ? I venture to say that not a man in England would consent to the appointment of any man not an Englishman. Territory should be in the keeping of men living on the soil and no other man should be permitted to dispose of it. Therefore I say that the government of Canada made an extraordinary mistake and a mistake which will become more apparent as it becomes more fully understood by the people of Canada. It is no use hiding from ourselves the fact that the diplomacy of England in North America for sixty years has been weak. I have heard the Prime Minister himself say that he was not in

sympathy with the diplomacy of England on this" continent. Therefore you were warned and notified that the British diplomacy was weak, and when you had the opportunity of removing it to Canadian diplomacy you should have done so. What is the use of being forewarned if you are not forearmed ? Why did you not insist ? Had I been more familiar with the procedure in this House the first year I was here I would have moved that three Canadians be appointed on the committee. However, when I heard the Prime Minister say that he was no lover of British diplomacy on this continent I thought that when he had the choice he would have had three Canadians and if he had had three Canadians we would not have had this difficulty to-day.
Another thing that lias struck me is the fact that there was never any suspicion about the United States commissioners giving in or losing in this arbitration. There was not a word of that kind in their press or the press of England ; they all took it for granted that the. United States commissioners would stick to their case. The just settlement of this question is the just settlement of the relations of England and this country and in the settlement of this question we must ascertain whether the English government has done us wrong in not looking after our territory or whether the fault lies at the door of the Canadian government.
I would prefer that it should lie here, even if the right hon. gentleman should escape the auger of public opinion in order that ^ it might not create feelings that might prejudice the existence of the empire. Therefore I want to know why it is that from the very moment Lord Alverstone's name was mentioned it was stated in the American papers, professedly inspired, that Lord Alver-stone was to decide in favour of the United States. There must have been some agreement between the government of England and the government of Canada that the government of Canada was to consent to the sacrifice of Canada in order to serve some supposed imperial policy. It is clear to my mind that it was communicated from the Foreign Office in London to the Secretary of State in Washington that the United States had nothing to fear, to go on with the treaty that England would appoint a man who would decide the case in favour of the United States, as England wanted to get rid of the case and to preserve the friendship of the United States, and that England was willing to sacrifice the interests of Canada and had succeeded in getting the government of Canada to accede.
Does my hon. friend say that seriously ?

I believe that in some way or other the government of Canada was overcome by the government of England. The thing was rigged in this way. They said to the government of Canada : You can ap-

point two Canadians and let the Chief Justice of England be appointed as well ; the Chief Justice of England will decide in favour of the United States, your tfwo people can dissent, that will protect you in Canada and settle this question for the empire and relieve us of a great difficulty. However there is no doubt that the people will arrive at as correct a conclusion in this matter when it has been fully explained to them, as any logician. Public opinion invariably forms a conclusion better than a logician of the character of Goldwin Smith, who always goes wrong although he is a trained logician.
Does my hon. friend pretend to say there was a secret agreement ?
I was reasoning from the facts.
My hon. friend is all wrong.

Then how did the United States get the knowledge as soon as Lord Alverstone was appointed that he was going to decide for them ? And now as a matter of fact after he has decided for them I undertake to say that the State Department at Washington had some information from some source, that he was to decide for them.
That I do not know.

We must understand the whole question from beginning to end and I do not believe that Lord Alverstone is to blame ; I believe that he was appointed on that commission with instructions, in the interest of the empire, to give the award that he has given.
Does my hon. friend know that Lord Alverstone had to take an oath that he would interpret the treaty judicially ? And does he think that in the face of that

The Englishman's idea of ' judicial interpretation ' would be to serve the interests of the empire. I want to call the attention of the Prime Minister to the fact that he must have known-he did know -of the extraordinary opinion in England with regard to the importance of the good will of the United States to the empire. That opinion is incorrect. The people of England have more to gain by sticking to Canada than by kow-towing to the United States; yet, I do not find a single word in this correspondence calling the attention of the English government to that fact. There is the clearest evidence, on the contrary, that this government permitted that opinion in Great Britain to go on, and become stronger day by day. If this government wish to serve the empire, they should let the people of England know that they must look to Canada for their support
on this continent, and not to the United States. Every time they sacrifice the interests of Canada, in order to conciliate the United States, the people of the United States become more greedy and grasping, and the people of this country become more alarmed and dissatisfied.
There must have been some understanding, somewhere and somehow, that the commission would uphold the contentions of the United States. Why, the determination of this tribunal was known in the United States three months before it was announced. And three, four or five days before Lord Alverstone had given his decision, the finding of this commission was announced accurately and in wonderful detail in the press of the United States. I intend to investigate this question. I intend to follow it ' secundum artem.' Three, four or five days before the decision, as soon as the argument was closed, announcements were made in the United States as to what the decision would be. How did the facts gets out of Lord Alverstone's head and into the heads of the Yankee newspaper men and the Yankee commissioners ? Tell me that, if you can, There is only one conclusion-this was a triumph of the diplomacy of England over the government of Canada. The government of Canada had the matter in their own hands; and, if the interests of Canada have been sacrificed, they must bear the responsibility. They had full power to negotiate, and now that the interests of Canada have been sacrificed, the hon. member for Labelle (Mr. Bourassa) is put up, to charge that upon the British government, and the Prime Minister follows him, virtually in support of the same idea.
There is just one other remark of the Prime Minister to which I wish to refer. He said that the United States was a populous and powerful country, and that Canada was a small colony. If the government of England had attempted to thrust upon us a treaty that was not in accordance with Canada's rights the Prime Minister could have summoned this parliament and there would have been such an expression of public indignation that the government in England would have backed down. All he had to do was to summon this faithful Commons and we would soon teach the English government that they could not thrust upon this country any treaty made to suit the diplomacy of the United States. If this colony is treated in that way, let not the Prime Minister say that it is because it is a weak colony. England would have stuck to us, if we had asserted our rights and demanded the protection of the imperial parliament. We are not a weak colony. Six milions of free people would beat the United States single-handed in the contest. If we fought them as the Swiss people fought the power of Austria, we should beat them to a stand-still. We are a powerful

people, and occupy the best strategic position on this continent.
We beat them in 1812, when they were relatively forty times as populous as they are now.

Of course. And we could do it again. It is not right for the Frime Minister to seek to weaken the great public sentiment of Canada by saying that we are not able to cope with the invader.
"If we had shown that we were prepared to fight for ourselves, England would have been at our back with her forces and the United States would never have dared to attempt to capture our territory. Therefore, notwithstanding all that has been said, I claim that the government of Canada alone are responsible in this matter. Sir. Chamberlain, in writing, made suggestions. He had a right, as a British statesman, to give his private opinion. Just as I might advise a client that it would be better to compromise rather than fight for his rights. But it would be the right of the client to refuse to compromise. Sir. Chamberlain had a right to make suggestions to the government, but the government were independent men and representatives of Canada, and they should have at once replied : We cannot stand for any sacrifice of the rights of Canada.
As to the Bulwer-Clayton treaty, I think my leader (Sir. Borden) put that matter in the right light. We had the opportunity to get the help of England and to have our rights maintained. But the right bon. Premier of this country took the unexampled course of saying that we had no interest in that treaty. That is a treaty affecting this continent; and, on whatever continent there Is a British colony, any treaty affecting that continent affects that part of the British empire, and the colony should assert its rights as part of the British empire. And, when we told the English government that we had no interest in this matter, it sho-wed that we had not the high appreciation of our rights that we ought to have.
I am glad of this debate. It would have been unfortunate if the people of England had been led to fancy that a decision like this could be given, and the people of Canada not resent it. I am glad that the press of Canada have shown to the world that our spirit is not daunted, that we are not weaklings, but that we are of a proud race, that we possess the daring qualities of that race in the highest degree, and that our strength is not sapped by luxury or decay. I am glad to see that the press of England are speaking out for Canada. And, in view of the temper of the people of England, as exhibited through their press, it would be a most unfortunate spectacle for the world had Canada remained silent. When this debate is reported in England to-morrow the press of England will assist, as far as possible, in educating the people of Eng-Mr. GOURLEY.
land with reference to the position we occupy in the British empire. I thank the House for the consideration they have given ray remarks.

The managers on the part of the House of Commons withdrew their objections to the Senate amendments Nos. 2, 3, 4 and 70 to sections 5. 6, 7 and 310 of the said Bill.

speakername: The PRIME MINISTER (Rt. Hon. Sir Wilfrid Laurier).

speechtext:
As the House is about to adjourn, I would crave permission to draw attention to an article which appears in to-day's Montreal ' Star ' and which reads as follows :
One of the privileges of a member of the House of Commons is that of saying anything he pleases on the floor of the House without being held to account for what he says before the courts of law.
He may say that which is grossly untrue and slanderous. He may be animated by envy, hatred, malice and all uncharitableness. He may be actuated by a d'esire for personal or party .advantage, or simply by a desire for notoriety He may say just what he pleases without fear [DOT]of the law.
Such a privilege would in itself serve as a restraint upon the tongue of a high principled man.
Unfortunately, all members of parliament are not high principled, and slanders are frequently uttered on the floor of the House with a recklessness. which is born of immunity from legal consequence.	,
Three weeks ago that eminent jurist, Mr. Talbot, of Bellechasse, declared on the floor of the House that two of the petitions against the Grand Trunk Pacific scheme were forged. Sir Wilfrid Laurie# promptly followed this up by a declaration that the same charge would apply to most of the petitions. Mr. Talbot moved that two of tho petitions should be referred to the Committee on Privileges and Elections for investigation, and Mr. Borden suggested in amendment that all the petitions should be referred to the Committee. Sir Wilfrid, in a moment of weakness, accepted the amendment. There the matter rests. The Committee met once ; formally passed a resolution asking permission to sit while the House was in session, and has never met again.
The whole thing was a bluff ; the charges were .a bluff ; the reference to the committee was a
bluff. The ' Star,' at the time, denounced the whole business as a bluff and expressed the opinion that the government would never dare to have the charges investigated.
The privileges of parliament were never intended to cover such infamous cowardice ; and if used for such purposes the sooner they are abolished the better. The genuineness of the petitions is beyond question, beyond suspicion. If any names at all were forged, they were probably forged ^ by friends of the government anxious to diminish the influence of the vast mass of genuine signatures sent in to parliament. The important and all-significent fact is that the government dared not allow an investigation of the charges it made with such reckless and splendid courage.
Now, Mr. Speaker, it may be that when I made that motion I made a mistake.
Does the hon. gentleman intend to make a motion ?

I intend to move tho adjournment of the House. It may be said at this late stage of the session I was wrong in bringlnig that matter up, but I could not have made it any sooner, for you know as well as I do that these petitions were brought into the House at the very tail end of the discussion of the Transcontinental Railway. On the very day these petitions were read in the House, I drew attention to their character, expressing my doubt as to the authenticity of the signatures. Now, I have in my possession documents to prove that I was perfectly justified in making my motion, although it was so late in the session. I have now in my possession nine affidavits

I object to my hon. friend going into a matter that is before a Committee of the House. I have not the slightest objection to the investigation going on before the committee, but to read affidavits in the House about a matter that has been referred to a committee, is I submit, out of order.
The question is quite new to me. I know there are some authorities upon it.

It cannot be a matter that would require very much authority. A question respecting petitions presented to this House which has been raised as a question of privilege surely cannot be considered by this House while it is subject to the jurisdiction of a committee or until that committee has reported. Otherwise it would be competent for every hon. member in this House to bring in affidavits on one side or the other and to contest in this House the question which has been referred to the committee for the purpose of report. That would be a very elementary principle upon which to act.

I think the hon. gentleman (Mr. Borden, Halifax) should be the last man in the world to rise in this House and attempt to prevent a member who, in one of

the most important papers in Canada, is called a coward and a slanderer from availing himself of the only opportunity he has of defending himself. I think I should be allowed that privilege.

I am not preventing my hon. friend from defending himself in any way. As soon as he made his motion in the House, I rose in my place and said, that, in view of the statements he made, I would unqualifiedly support a reference to the committee. The hon. gentleman has had the matter referred to the committee. It is now under the control of the committee. It has not been proceeded with. What I am objecting to is that my hon. friend should undertake to proceed to deal by means of affidavits with a matter which has been referred to a committee of the House for investigation and report.
Mr. Speaker, if you will permit me
Order, order.

Perhaps we may settle this question which has been raised by the hon. leader of the opposition. I will not read the affidavits but I will give a personal explanation if I am allowed to do so. ^ I have in my possession thirteen affidavits, nine of them proving that the signatures on these petitions were not authorized in any way by the persons whose names appear upon them.
Mr. Speaker, my hon. friend

And I have four of them showing that signatures were on the petitions of men who are living in the United States at the present time.
Mr. BORDEN (Halifax. I do not think it is a very worthy course on the part of my hon. friend, when a point of order has been raised, to evade it by stating the substance of the affidavits instead of reading them. It seems to me a very plain point of order that when the matter raised by my hon. friend has been referred to a committee lie should not endeavour by affidavits to deal with the very same question in the House, because to permit that, would be to permit every member of the House to bring in affidavits pro and con which would take away from the committee the functions which it was designed they should exercise under the reference thereto, and it is as much out of order to state the substance of the affidavits as to read them. To rise for the ostensible purpose of speaking on a point of order and then to endeavour to evade the point of order is not a worthy thing for a member of the House to do, and it is not respectful to Mr. Speaker.
I find that the principle generally laid down is that when a question is referred to a committee, the House

has no right to deal with the matter itself, but the hon. member (Mr. Talbot)-perhaps the hon. gentleman (Mr. Borden, Halifax) was not in when lie read the statement-has read a statement from a paper reflecting upon his character and upon his reputation as a member of this House. I suppose, if the hon. gentleman wants simply to state the reasons why he brought this question up without entering into the merits of the petitions which have been referred to the committee, he may do so.

That is my iutention. I merely want to state that when I brought this matter before the House, I was justified in doing so, because I have in my possession documents sworn to which justify me as a member of this House in stating that the privilege of this Plouse was grossly abused, probably without the knowledge of hon. members at the time, and which go to prove the statement which I made at the time that half the names were forged. I have documents to prove it, and consequently I say that there is no foundation for the statements which the 'Star has made, and that the position I took at the time was perfectly correct, according to the facts as disclosed in the documents.
I beg to move the adjournment of the House.

As a member of the committee to which this matter was referred, I beg to inform you, Mr. Speaker, and the House, that the committee was called together many days ago, immediately after the reference. The hon. gentleman (Mr. Talbot) had the opportunity of bringing that matter up, but from the time the committee met to the present hour we have never heard one word in support of the charge. The hon. gentleman has made no effort to bring the matter forward. He has made no effort to have the committee take action upon it, and we have never heard a word from the hon. gentleman as to the evidence in support of these charges.
The article was only printed to-day.
I hope the hon. gentleman (Mr. Talbot) will withdraw his motion, because we may have a motion to adjourn when there is nothing before the House.
I will withdraw the motion.

Before the motion is withdrawn, I would like to say that my hon. friend (Mr. Talbot) made his statement on the 7th of October, that he has had some fifteen days in which to prove his charges and that up to the present time they have not been proved. My hon. friend will recollect that when he made his motion, I rose and said that I concurred heartily in it. The right hon. Prime Minister then rose in his place and said :

But as there is an impression growing very strong in the country, that in fact there has been an attempt at a conspiracy to impose upon this House. I am perfectly willing to excuse my hon. friend's language.
